title: Romans 8:28 in Context
description: What Romans 8:28 actually says: God works in all things for good, for those who love him. Not that everything is good, and not a promise of a happy ending on your timeline.
tagline: “All things work together for good” has a second half most people skip.
context: Paul has just spent a paragraph on suffering: creation groaning, believers groaning, the Spirit interceding “with groanings which can’t be uttered” because we don’t even know what to pray. That is the setting for verse 28. It isn’t a cheerful verse dropped into a cheerful chapter; it’s the turn in a passage about pain. Notice what it does and doesn’t claim. It doesn’t say all things are good. It says God works in all things toward good, and it says this for a specific group: those who love God, who are called according to his purpose. The next verses define the “good”: being shaped into the likeness of Christ. That is a much larger and slower promise than a job offer or a clean scan.
misread: Quoted as “everything happens for a reason” or as a guarantee that a hard situation will turn out well. Paul says neither. He says God is at work in the situation, and that the eventual good is who you become, not necessarily what you get.
use: Good for someone who needs to know that their suffering isn’t wasted. Not good as a quick answer to someone in fresh grief; it can sound like the loss was a means to an end. Read verses 26–27 with it so the groaning is included.

title: Jeremiah 29:11 in Context
description: Jeremiah 29:11 was written to exiles who would stay in Babylon for seventy years. What “plans for your welfare” meant to them, and what it can mean for you.
tagline: It was a letter to people who weren’t going home.
context: Jeremiah sends this line in a letter to Jews who have just been deported to Babylon. False prophets are telling them the exile will be short. Jeremiah tells them the opposite: build houses, plant gardens, marry, seek the good of the city, because you will be there seventy years. Then comes verse 11. The “plans” are plans for the nation across generations, and the “expected end” is a return most of the letter’s first readers would not live to see. Read that way, the verse is not a promise of a prosperous year. It is a promise that a long, undeserved wait is not abandonment.
misread: Used on graduation cards and in job searches as a personal guarantee of prosperity and a hopeful near future. The verse is addressed to a nation, and its hope is seventy years out.
use: It still works, with the setting included. The principle that carries is this: God’s intentions toward his people are good even when the circumstances say otherwise, and the timeline is his. Offer it to someone in a long wait, and be honest about what it promised the first time.

title: Philippians 4:13 in Context
description: “I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me” comes at the end of a passage about being content with little. It is about endurance, not achievement.
tagline: Paul wrote it from a prison, about having nothing.
context: Paul is thanking the Philippians for a gift of money, and he wants to say thank you without sounding like he was desperate. So he explains: he has learned to be content whether he has plenty or nothing, whether he is full or hungry. Then verse 13: I can do all things through him who strengthens me. The “all things” in context are the two just named, abundance and want. The verse is a statement about surviving either without losing his footing. It is one of the most quoted verses in sports, and it has nothing to do with winning.
misread: Printed on athletic gear as a promise of success. Paul is describing the strength to endure lack, not the strength to achieve.
use: For someone facing scarcity, illness, or a season of doing without, this is the right verse, read with verses 11–12. For someone about to compete or interview, it still applies, but the strength on offer is to handle the outcome either way, not to secure the outcome you want.

title: Psalm 46:10 in Context
description: “Be still, and know that I am God” is said in the middle of a psalm about earthquakes and war. Its stillness is a command to stop fighting, not a mood.
tagline: It is closer to “stand down” than “relax.”
context: Psalm 46 opens with mountains falling into the sea and nations in uproar. God’s response, in verse 9, is to break bows and shatter spears. Then verse 10, spoken by God: Be still, and know that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations. The Hebrew for “be still” means to let go, to drop your hands. It is addressed to the warring nations as much as to the frightened worshiper: stop striving, and recognize who is actually in charge. That gives the verse more weight than a meditation prompt. It is stillness in the presence of someone who can end the fight.
misread: Used as a quiet-time verse about calming your mind. It can be that, but the stillness in the psalm is surrender in a crisis, not silence in a peaceful room.
use: Right for someone who is exhausting themselves trying to control a situation. Read the whole psalm; the refuge in verse 1 and the river in verse 4 are what make the stillness possible.

title: 1 Corinthians 10:13 in Context
description: The verse behind “God won’t give you more than you can handle.” It is about temptation, and it promises a way out, not a limit on suffering.
tagline: The saying isn’t in the Bible. This is the verse people are thinking of.
context: Paul has just recounted Israel’s failures in the wilderness as a warning to the Corinthians: don’t assume you’re safe. Then verse 13: no temptation has taken you but what is common to humanity, and God won’t allow you to be tempted beyond your ability, but will provide the way of escape. The subject is temptation, the pull toward doing wrong. The promise is that you will never be in a situation where sin is the only option. It is not a promise about the size of your burdens. Paul himself says in 2 Corinthians 1:8 that he was burdened beyond his strength, so that he despaired even of life.
misread: Reworded as a guarantee that suffering is capped at what you can bear. Paul says the opposite about suffering elsewhere, and this verse isn’t about suffering at all.
use: Use it for someone facing a specific temptation: an addiction, an affair, dishonesty at work. For someone crushed by circumstances, reach for Psalm 34:18 or 2 Corinthians 1:8–9 instead, which are honest that the weight can exceed us.

title: Proverbs 22:6 in Context
description: “Train up a child in the way he should go” is a proverb, a general observation about how life usually goes. It was never a guarantee about any particular child.
tagline: Proverbs describe patterns. They don’t sign contracts.
context: Proverbs is a collection of sayings about how the world generally works: the diligent usually prosper, the hot-tempered usually make trouble, careful parenting usually produces a steady adult. “Usually” is built into the genre. The same book says a gentle answer turns away wrath, which is true most of the time and not always. Verse 6 sits in a run of such observations. Read as a promise, it has broken the hearts of faithful parents whose children walked away. Read as a proverb, it is an encouragement that patient formation tends to hold, and a warning that neglect tends not to.
misread: Treated as a guarantee, which then becomes an accusation: if your adult child has left the faith, you must have trained them wrong. The verse makes no such claim.
use: Encourage a parent with it, but say what it is. If you are talking with a parent grieving a child’s choices, this is not the verse to bring. Luke 15 is.

title: Matthew 6:34 in Context
description: “Don’t be anxious for tomorrow” ends a passage about birds and lilies. Jesus doesn’t say tomorrow will be easy; he says today’s trouble is enough to carry.
tagline: The last line of a ten-verse argument about worry.
context: From verse 25 Jesus has been making a case: look at the birds, who don’t farm and are fed; look at the lilies, who don’t weave and are clothed; you are worth more than either. He names the things people worry about, food, drink, clothing, and says the Father already knows you need them. Verse 33 gives the alternative: seek the kingdom first. Then 34 lands the point. Don’t borrow tomorrow’s trouble. Tomorrow will have its own, and there will be provision for it then. The verse doesn’t deny that hard things are coming. It refuses to pay for them twice.
misread: Reduced to “don’t worry, be happy.” Jesus assumes trouble; his instruction is about which day’s trouble you carry.
use: For chronic worriers, this is the verse, and the whole passage from verse 25 should be read slowly. The birds and lilies are the argument; verse 34 alone is only the conclusion.

title: Psalm 23 in Context
description: Psalm 23 is confident because of who the shepherd is, not because the road is safe. It walks through a dark valley and eats in front of enemies.
tagline: The most familiar psalm is more honest about danger than people remember.
context: A shepherd’s psalm written by a former shepherd, and the setting matters: sheep are led to pasture and water because they can’t find them alone, and through the valley because there is no way around it. Verse 4 assumes the valley. Verse 5 sets a table with enemies watching. The confidence of the psalm isn’t that nothing bad will happen; it is that the shepherd goes ahead, carries a rod against predators and a staff to pull the sheep back, and doesn’t leave. Read at funerals because it doesn’t flinch at the “shadow of death,” and read before surgery for the same reason.
misread: Heard as a lullaby. It’s a psalm for people walking through something.
use: Works almost anywhere: hospitals, funerals, sleepless nights. Read it whole; the six verses are one movement from pasture to table to home.

title: Isaiah 41:10 in Context
description: “Don’t be afraid, for I am with you” was said to exiles facing the most powerful empire on earth. Five promises in one verse, and the last one is a hand.
tagline: Said to people with every reason to be afraid.
context: Isaiah 40–48 is addressed to Israel in Babylon, small, defeated, and surrounded by a superpower. Chapter 41 pictures the nations trembling at a coming conqueror, and then turns to Israel: but you, my servant, whom I have chosen. Verse 10 gives five promises in quick succession: I am with you, I am your God, I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you. The last is the most physical: a right hand that holds you up. The verse doesn’t promise the empire will go away. It promises a grip that won’t.
misread: Rarely misread, but often quoted without the people it was said to. Knowing they were captives makes “don’t be afraid” a braver thing to say.
use: One of the best verses for fear of any kind, and short enough to memorize. Good before surgery, before a hard conversation, and for anyone who feels small against something large.

title: John 14:27 in Context
description: Jesus gives his peace the night before his arrest, to friends who are about to scatter. It is explicitly not the world’s kind of peace.
tagline: Given hours before everything fell apart.
context: This is the upper room, the last evening. Jesus has washed feet, predicted a betrayal and a denial, and told the disciples he is leaving. They are frightened and confused. Into that he says: peace I leave with you, my peace I give to you, not as the world gives. The world’s peace is the absence of trouble; his is something that holds while trouble is happening, and he says so knowing what the next day holds for him and for them. “Don’t let your heart be troubled” is a command he gives to people whose hearts have every reason to be.
misread: Treated as a promise that things will calm down. The disciples’ circumstances got worse, not better, within hours.
use: For someone in the middle of something, not after it. It pairs well with Philippians 4:6–7, which describes the same peace as a guard.

title: Philippians 4:6–7 in Context
description: Paul’s instruction for anxiety is a practice, not a feeling: turn each worry into a request, add thanks, and let peace stand guard. Written from prison.
tagline: A method, written by a man awaiting a verdict.
context: Paul writes Philippians from custody, not knowing whether he will be released or executed; he weighs both possibilities in chapter 1. So “in nothing be anxious” is not advice from a comfortable chair. What he offers is concrete. In everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, make your requests known. Then a result: the peace of God, which surpasses understanding, will guard your hearts and thoughts. The image is a sentry posted at the door of the mind. The peace doesn’t require the situation to be resolved. It arrives before the verdict.
misread: Read as “stop feeling anxious,” a command about emotion. Paul gives a sequence of actions and describes what follows them.
use: For anyone lying awake with a list of worries: take each one and turn it into a specific request, then name one thing you are thankful for. The verse works best as something done rather than read.

title: Matthew 18:20 in Context
description: “Where two or three are gathered” is said in a passage about a church confronting a member who has done wrong. It is about authority in hard conversations, not about small attendance.
tagline: It is said about church discipline, not about small meetings.
context: Matthew 18:15–20 lays out what to do when a fellow believer sins against you: go privately, then take one or two others, then tell the church. Verses 18–20 back up that process with authority: what the gathered believers bind and loose is bound and loosed, and where two or three gather in Jesus’ name, he is there. The small number is the two or three witnesses from verse 16. The promise of presence is real, but it is a promise about a difficult, careful confrontation done rightly, with Jesus among those doing it.
misread: Used to reassure a small prayer meeting that God shows up when few people come. He does, but this verse is about something more specific and more demanding.
use: Best for people entering a hard conversation of accountability, especially in a church setting. For encouragement about small gatherings, Acts 2:42–47 is a better fit.

title: 1 Corinthians 13 in Context
description: “Love is patient, love is kind” was written to a church that was fighting. It is a correction before it is a wedding reading.
tagline: Written to a church in conflict, not to a couple in love.
context: The Corinthian church was divided over leaders, suing each other, arguing about spiritual gifts, and humiliating the poor at the Lord’s Supper. Chapter 13 sits between two chapters on spiritual gifts and answers the question of what those gifts are for. Every line of “love is” is a description of what the Corinthians were not being: patient, kind, not envious, not boastful, not rude, not self-seeking. It is one of the most beautiful passages in the Bible and it was written as a rebuke. Which is why it works at a wedding: it describes love as something you do when it is hard, not something you feel when it is easy.
misread: Read as a sentimental description of romance. It is a demanding standard aimed at people who were failing it.
use: Excellent for weddings if the couple is told what it is. Also the right passage for a church, a family, or a team in conflict.

title: Psalm 34:18 in Context
description: “Near to those who have a broken heart” was written after David escaped by pretending to be insane. It is comfort from the floor, not from a throne.
tagline: David wrote it after one of his worst days.
context: The heading of Psalm 34 tells us the setting: David, on the run from Saul, has fled to a Philistine king and, recognized and in danger, saves his life by acting like a madman, drooling into his beard. It is not a dignified story. The psalm he writes afterward is about a God who hears the cry of the humiliated. Verse 18 says God is near to the brokenhearted and saves those crushed in spirit. Notice the order: the nearness is a response to the breaking, not a reward for recovering. You don’t have to be put back together first.
misread: Rarely misread; more often quoted without the story, which is what makes it credible.
use: One of the best sympathy-card verses because it requires nothing of the reader but being broken. Read the whole psalm to someone who has been humiliated as well as hurt.

title: Matthew 11:28–30 in Context
description: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened” offers rest, and then a yoke. Jesus isn’t promising less work; he’s promising a burden that fits.
tagline: The rest comes with a yoke. That’s the point.
context: Jesus has just been rejected by the towns where he did most of his miracles and is about to clash with the religious leaders over Sabbath rules. Between those, he turns to the tired. Come to me, and I will give you rest. Then, oddly: take my yoke. A yoke is a tool for work, fitted to an animal’s shoulders so the load can be pulled. The rest on offer is not the absence of a load but a load that fits, carried alongside someone gentle. The contrast is with the religious leaders, who Jesus later says tie up heavy burdens and won’t lift a finger.
misread: Heard as a promise of a lighter schedule. It is a promise of a different master.
use: For the exhausted, especially the religiously exhausted. It pairs with Psalm 23’s “he makes me lie down.”

title: John 3:16 in Context
description: The most famous verse in the Bible is part of a night conversation with a religious leader who came to Jesus in secret. It answers a question he was afraid to ask.
tagline: Said quietly, at night, to one man.
context: Nicodemus is a Pharisee and a member of the ruling council, and he comes to Jesus after dark, presumably so no one will see. Jesus tells him he must be born again, which Nicodemus doesn’t understand, and then explains how: as Moses lifted up the bronze serpent in the wilderness so that anyone who looked at it lived, the Son of Man will be lifted up. Verse 16 follows. God loved the world in this way: he gave his one and only Son, so that whoever believes will not perish. The verse is universal in scope and personal in setting, said to a frightened, careful man who eventually helped bury Jesus.
misread: Not so much misread as detached. Stadium signs make it a slogan; the chapter makes it an answer to a real person’s fear.
use: Read verses 1–21 to anyone who thinks they know this verse. It is better with Nicodemus in the room.

title: Ecclesiastes 3:1 in Context
description: “To everything there is a season” is the Bible’s most read funeral passage. What the list of times is actually saying, and why it comforts people of any belief.
tagline: A time for everything, including the things nobody wants a time for.
context: Ecclesiastes is the Bible’s most unsparing book, written by a teacher who has tried wealth, pleasure, and wisdom and found them all “vapor.” Chapter 3 opens with fourteen pairs: born and die, plant and uproot, weep and laugh, mourn and dance, keep silent and speak. None of the pairs is called good or bad. They are simply the shape of a human life, laid out in order. The comfort of the passage is that it makes room for everything. There is a time to mourn, and it is not a failure. There is a time to dance, and it is not a betrayal of the mourning. The teacher does not promise that we will understand the timing; later in the chapter he says God has put eternity in our hearts but we cannot fathom what he has done from beginning to end.
misread: Read as fatalism (“it was just his time”) or as a promise that the good seasons are coming. It is neither. It is an honest inventory, and its comfort is that grief has a place in the design rather than being an interruption of it.
use: The right passage for a funeral when the room holds people of many beliefs or none, because it asks nothing of the listener. Read verses 1–8 slowly. Also good, quietly, for someone in a season they did not choose.

title: Isaiah 40:31 in Context
description: “They who wait for Yahweh will renew their strength.” Written to exiles who thought God had lost track of them. What waiting means here, and why the strength comes in the waiting rather than after it.
tagline: The eagle, the running, and the walking are in descending order on purpose.
context: Isaiah 40 is addressed to Israel in exile, who have concluded that God has forgotten them: “my way is hidden from Yahweh.” The chapter answers with a God who measures the oceans in his hand, names every star, and does not grow weary. Then it turns to the weary people: those who wait for him will renew their strength. Notice the order of the three images. Mount up with wings like eagles; run and not be weary; walk and not faint. It goes down, not up. Soaring is the exception; most of a hard season is walking without fainting, and the verse says that, too, is renewed strength. The waiting is not a delay before the strength arrives. It is where the strength is found.
misread: Used as a promise of triumph (the eagle) and quoted in athletic settings. The passage is about exhausted, forgotten people getting enough to keep walking.
use: For the long middle of anything: illness, a job search, caregiving. For someone who has stopped expecting to soar and just needs to not faint, this is the verse, and it is honest with them.

title: Lamentations 3:22–23 in Context
description: “New every morning” was written in a burned city by someone who had lost everything. Why that setting is what makes the verse trustworthy.
tagline: Written with the city still smoking.
context: Lamentations is five poems of grief over the destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon: the temple burned, the walls down, the people deported or dead. The writer, traditionally Jeremiah, does not soften any of it; the book includes lines about children starving. Chapter 3 is the center, and it is the only place hope appears. He has just said “my strength and my hope have perished.” Then: it is because of Yahweh’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed; they are new every morning. He is not saying things are fine. He is saying that waking up at all, in the ruins, is evidence that God has not finished with him. That is a far stronger claim than optimism, because of where it was made.
misread: Put on sunrise photographs as a general cheerfulness. It is a statement made in the worst circumstances in the Old Testament, and it means the most to people in the worst circumstances now.
use: For the first mornings after a loss, a breakup, a diagnosis, when waking up means remembering. Not as a promise the day will be good, but that you were not abandoned in the night.
